headline: Recognized-firm audits (ChainSecurity + Spearbit) cover core ALM contracts; public GitHub repo confirmed — but no deployed addresses were discoverable this run, leaving on-chain bytecode verification status unconfirmed

findings.text: No deployed contract addresses were discoverable in this run (address_book is null; raw GitHub address registry was access-blocked; block explorer pages could not be fetched). Bytecode verification status on Ethereum, Base, Optimism, Arbitrum, Avalanche, and Unichain is therefore unconfirmed. This is the principal gap preventing a green grade.

Public source-code repository confirmed at https://github.com/sparkdotfi/spark-alm-controller covering ALMProxy.sol, MainnetController.sol, ForeignController.sol, RateLimits.sol, and RateLimitHelpers.sol. No deployed-addresses artifact was successfully fetched, so a deploy-commit SHA could not be pinned.

ChainSecurity audit dated 2024-10-22 covers core ALM contracts at final commit 6058f68f79520eb06ea8eded146da13039c47525 (Bump Version). Scope includes ALMProxy.sol, ForeignController.sol, MainnetController.sol, RateLimitHelpers.sol, RateLimits.sol, and deployment scripts. Zero critical/high/medium/low findings remain open; 7 informational findings all resolved. GitHub releases page also describes v1.1.0 (December 2024) as 'Production release, audited by Spearbit and ChainSecurity', covering added AAVE support and ERC-4626 generalization — indicating follow-up audit coverage for the material feature additions.

Both auditing firms are broadly recognized: ChainSecurity (Decentralized Security AG) is on the recognized-firms list. Spearbit is also on the recognized-firms list. A third reviewer 'PullUp' is mentioned in release notes but not a recognized firm per the rubric — it appears to be a supplementary review, not the primary audit.

The ChainSecurity audit commit (6058f68f, 22 Oct 2024) predates the v1.1.0 production release (December 2024), which adds AAVE deposit/withdraw and ERC-4626 generalizations. However, the GitHub releases page explicitly labels v1.1.0 as 'Production release, audited by Spearbit and ChainSecurity', and release notes reference Spearbit-specific fixes. This indicates the material post-October changes were covered by a follow-up Spearbit + ChainSecurity review. The Spearbit audit PDF was not fetched this run, so exact scope commit is unknown.

The 'ALMProxy' contract is named proxy but functions as a fund-custody executor using OpenZeppelin AccessControl — it is NOT an EIP-1967/transparent/UUPS upgradeable proxy. Controllers (MainnetController, ForeignController) are non-upgradeable by design per audit and docs. No EIP-1967 proxy pattern was identified in the audited scope; proxy-vs-implementation verification split is not applicable. However, without addresses, this cannot be confirmed on-chain.

steelman.red: No deployed contract addresses were found in this run, making it impossible to confirm bytecode is verified on any block explorer — a protocol whose deployed code cannot be independently inspected on-chain is effectively unverified from an outsider's perspective.
steelman.orange: While audits from two recognized firms (ChainSecurity, Spearbit) cover the core contracts and a public GitHub repo exists, the absence of verified on-chain bytecode evidence — due to undiscoverable addresses this run — means only off-chain source-level verification is confirmed, placing the protocol firmly in the orange tier where audit scope adequacy is satisfied but on-chain verification is unconfirmed.
steelman.green: The v1.1.0 production release is explicitly described as audited by both Spearbit and ChainSecurity, the public GitHub repo is active and matches the described contract architecture, all informational findings in the ChainSecurity audit were resolved, and the protocol likely has verified source on Etherscan given it is operated by SparkDAO (a mature team) — if addresses were fetched and showed verification, green would be the natural grade.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because: the strongest green argument rests on an assumption ('likely verified') rather than fetched evidence — V1 (on-chain bytecode verification) cannot be confirmed without addresses, which were not discoverable this run. The orange steel-man accurately characterizes what was verified: audit quality and repo existence are confirmed from recognized firms, but the on-chain verification link is missing. Red would require that the audit or repo be absent, which is not the case here.

evidence.shows: Spark docs security page listing Spark ALM Controller audit repository at https://github.com/sparkdotfi/spark-alm-controller/tree/master/audits; confirms ChainSecurity and Spearbit as auditors for the Spark Liquidity Layer component

Files in scope: ALMProxy.sol, ForeignController.sol, MainnetController.sol, RateLimitHelpers.sol, RateLimits.sol, plus deployment scripts. Bytecode verification status on block explorers is therefore unconfirmed. Next run should inherit addresses from https://github.com/sparkdotfi/spark-address-registry/tree/master/src and fetch /api/contract/abi for each.

V2: Deploy-commit SHA for currently-deployed contracts could not be pinned — no deployed-addresses artifact was successfully fetched this run. Source-to-repo correspondence is inferred from public repo structure matching audited files, not from a pinned commit.
V3: Spearbit audit PDF URL for the v1.1.0 follow-up review (covering AAVE/ERC-4626 additions) was not fetched this run. Exact scope commit for Spearbit's review of v1.1.0 is unknown.

protocol_metadata.about: Spark Liquidity Layer (SLL) is an onchain capital allocator that manages liquidity flows for USDS and USDC between Ethereum mainnet and supported L2s (Base, Optimism, Arbitrum, Avalanche, Unichain). Users interact indirectly — the system mints/burns USDS via Sky's DSS Allocator, deposits into ERC-4626 vaults and Aave markets, swaps via the Spark PSM, and bridges using CCTP. The core mechanism is an ALMProxy (fund custody) controlled by governance-governed MainnetController and ForeignController contracts with per-operation rate limits enforced by a RateLimits contract.
